notes.h: Methods of payment for goods and services
notes.b: A household can pay for what it buys in several ways. Each method moves money differently, and knowing how each works lets you match the method to the purchase.
points: Cash: immediate payment in notes and coins. It is fast, costs nothing and shows exactly what has been spent, but carrying large amounts is unsafe, it leaves no record, and it cannot be used for online or distance purchases.

Cheque: a written order to the bank to pay a sum from the account to a named person. It requires a current account, takes time to clear, and can be refused if there are not enough funds. Cheques are used less now but are still examined.

Debit card: the amount is taken from the bank account straight away, so spending stays within the balance. It works by contactless or chip and PIN, and can be used online, for cashback and for ATM withdrawals.

Credit card: goods are bought now and paid for later, up to a credit limit. A minimum monthly payment is required, there is an interest-free period if the balance is cleared by the due date, and interest applies to any balance not cleared.
The card issuer may also protect some credit card purchases.
Direct debit: the account holder authorises a company or utility to take money from the account on a due date. The amount can vary, which suits bills such as utilities and insurance.

Standing order: the account holder instructs the bank to make a fixed payment at regular intervals to a named payee, such as rent, savings or loan repayments. The difference from direct debit is that the amount is fixed and the account holder controls the payment.

Online or mobile banking and payment apps: payments, bill payments and transfers made from a bank account through a computer or phone. They are convenient and keep a record, but need internet access and care with security.
Prepaid methods, gift vouchers and store credit are other ways to pay, where the money is paid in advance or held by one retailer.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain two methods of payment, giving what each does and one feature. For direct debit versus standing order, say that direct debit amounts can change while a standing order is fixed. Remember that a debit card takes money immediately but a credit card borrows.

notes.h: Criteria for choosing a payment method
notes.b: No single method is best for every purchase. A household compares methods against a set of criteria, then picks the one that suits the item and its own situation.
points: Cost: whether the method charges fees or interest, since this adds to the price of the goods.
Security: the risk of loss, theft or fraud, and whether the method leaves a record of the payment, which a cash payment does not.
Convenience: speed of payment, the ability to pay at a distance or online, and ease of budgeting.
Availability: whether the retailer or service provider accepts the method, and whether the buyer holds the card or account needed.
Control: whether the buyer can see and limit spending, which is easier with cash or a debit card than with credit, because credit lets you spend money you do not yet have.
Size of purchase: cash suits small everyday purchases, while credit or instalment methods suit large, expensive items the household cannot pay for at once, so the cost is spread.
notes.tip: You may be asked to suggest a method for a given purchase. For private health insurance, suggest direct debit or a card. For a car, suggest a loan or hire purchase. Give the reason that fits the household.

notes.h: Types of credit for household purchases
notes.b: Credit means obtaining goods, services or money now and paying later, usually with interest or charges. Households can use several different forms, each suited to a different need.
points: Credit card: a revolving credit facility (borrowing that can be reused as you repay) with a credit limit. It can offer an interest-free period if the full balance is paid on time.
Charge card: the full balance is due each month, and no interest is charged on it because it is repaid in full.
Store card: credit offered by a retailer, usable for purchases in that shop. It is usually costly.
Overdraft: the bank allows the current account balance to go below zero up to an agreed limit, with interest charged on the amount overdrawn. It is short-term and flexible but can be costly.

Personal or term loan from a bank, credit union or other lender: a fixed sum borrowed and repaid in fixed instalments over a set period at an agreed interest rate. It suits one-off large purchases such as a car.
Credit union loan: members can borrow from the credit union, usually after building up a savings record. Credit unions often have lower rates.
Other forms named in marking schemes: a budget account (spreads household bills), a credit sale, a moneylender (a licensed lender, usually very expensive) and a mortgage (a loan for house purchase).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name types of credit for household goods or for a car. Credit card, term loan, overdraft, hire purchase, store card and credit union loan are all good answers.

notes.b: Hire purchase lets a household use an expensive item straight away while paying for it over time. It is different from buying on a credit card, because ownership does not pass to the buyer at once.
points: Hire purchase combines hiring and buying: the buyer pays a deposit and then instalments over an agreed period, and uses the goods straight away.
The goods belong to the finance company until the final payment is made, so the buyer is only the hirer until then. Ownership passes to the buyer only at the last payment.
Once one-third or more of the total hire-purchase price has been paid, counting the deposit, instalments and the value of any trade-in, the owner cannot repossess the goods without a court order.
Before that point the owner must follow a procedure, including a default notice and time for the buyer to put things right. The buyer may also end the agreement.
Advantages: the goods can be used immediately, repayments are fixed and the cost is spread across instalments, so no large lump sum is needed.
Disadvantages: interest can make the total cost much higher than the cash price, and the buyer does not own the goods until the end.
Missed payments can lead to repossession. The goods may also lose value faster than the debt falls.
notes.tip: You may be asked to explain hire purchase with an advantage and a disadvantage, including the one-third and court order rule. Say that ownership stays with the finance company until the last instalment.

notes.b: Credit nearly always costs more than paying cash. To decide whether it is worth it, a household has to work out exactly how much extra it will pay.
points: Total cash price: the price of the goods if they are paid for in full at the time of purchase.
Total amount repayable: the deposit plus all the instalments paid under the credit agreement.
Cost of credit: the total amount repayable minus the cash price. It is the extra paid for the convenience of credit, so do not say the cost of credit is the total repayable.
Annual percentage rate (APR): the yearly cost of borrowing, as a percentage, including charges. Because every lender must express cost the same way, it allows different credit offers to be compared.
To compare cash and credit, the household adds all the payments, subtracts the cash price to find the cost of credit, and decides whether the immediate use of the goods is worth that extra cost.
notes.tip: Questions on comparing cash with credit need the cash price, the total repayable and the idea of APR. Subtract the cash price from the total repayable, and do not stop at the total.

notes.h: Advantages and disadvantages of using credit
notes.b: Credit can solve a real problem for a household, but it also carries costs and risks. Exam answers need both sides, each linked to the household.
points: Advantages: goods are available immediately, and large purchases become affordable because the cost is spread.
Advantages: credit can cover urgent or emergency costs, such as an emergency repair, and avoids the need to carry large amounts of cash, which is safer.
Advantages: loan repayments are fixed over a set period, so the cost is predictable, and a household can take advantage of sales. A good repayment record also helps later borrowing.
Disadvantages: interest makes goods cost more than the cash price, and high interest is charged if the credit balance is not repaid in full.
Disadvantages: credit makes overspending and impulse buying easier, and several credit agreements at once increase the risk of unmanageable debt.
Disadvantages: missed repayments can lead to penalties, repossession or a poor credit record, which makes future borrowing harder.
notes.tip: Exams ask for an advantage and a disadvantage of credit, or of credit for a car, utility bills or a family holiday. Link each point to the household, for example emergencies for an advantage and debt for a disadvantage.

notes.h: Factors to consider before taking credit
notes.b: Before signing a credit agreement, a household should check that the borrowing is sensible and that it can afford it. These are the questions to ask.
points: Whether the purchase is needed, because credit makes it easy to buy things that are only wanted.
The total cost, the interest rate and the APR, so that the offer can be compared with others and with the cash price.
The repayment amount and the length of the agreement, because a longer period usually means more interest in total.
Fees and penalties for missed payments.
Ownership, and what happens if repayments are missed, for example repossession under hire purchase.
Whether the repayments fit the household budget.
notes.tip: For the question on factors to consider when buying on credit, cover need, cost, interest, fees, repayment length, penalties and ownership.

notes.b: The Consumer Credit Act 1995 (as amended) is the law that protects people who borrow or buy on credit. It sets rules for lenders, so consumers know what they are agreeing to.
points: The Act protects consumers who buy on credit, including through hire purchase and other credit agreements. It regulates lenders, moneylenders and credit advertising, and the Central Bank of Ireland regulates the sector.
A credit agreement must be in writing and signed, and must set out the APR and the terms of repayment. The consumer must be given a copy.
The consumer has a short cooling-off period of 10 days after receiving a copy of the agreement to withdraw from it in writing.
Credit advertisements must be accurate and must show the APR, so offers can be compared.
For hire purchase, once one-third or more of the total price has been paid, the goods cannot be repossessed without a court order.

Where to get help: MABS (the Money Advice and Budgeting Service) and the Central Bank's consumer hub, the CCPC, and the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman for complaints about a bank or lender.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to outline the protection of the Consumer Credit Act 1995. Cover the written agreement, APR, copy, cooling-off period, advertising and hire-purchase protection, and get the Act's name right. Do not say that the Act bans credit or caps interest.

keyTerms.definition: Goods or services obtained now with payment deferred, usually with interest or charges applied.
An agreement to hire goods and pay for them in instalments, with ownership passing to the buyer only after the final payment.
The yearly cost of credit expressed as a percentage, including charges, used to compare credit offers.
The price of goods paid for in full at the time of purchase.
The total amount repayable under a credit agreement minus the cash price.
A card that takes payment directly from the holder's bank account.
A card that lets the holder buy now and pay later, subject to a credit limit and interest on any unpaid balance.
A payment authorised by the account holder that lets a company take a set amount from the account on a regular date.
A regular fixed payment made by the bank on the account holder's instruction.
An agreed facility that allows the account balance to go below zero up to an agreed limit.
Irish legislation, as amended, that protects consumers who buy on credit, including hire purchase.

factCards.term: What a credit advertisement must show
factCards.definition: It must be accurate and show the APR.
The buyer does not own the goods until the final payment; interest can make the total cost high; missed payments can lead to repossession.

Three types of credit for household goods
factCards.definition: Credit card, store card and hire purchase.

factCards.term: Two advantages of paying by cash
factCards.definition: It is fast and convenient, and the buyer can see exactly what has been spent.

questions.prompt: Describe how a hire-purchase agreement works for a household buying a washing machine, and state one risk the buyer faces.
questions.model: The buyer pays a deposit, then equal instalments over an agreed period. The buyer can use the machine immediately, but the finance company owns it until the final payment. Risk: if repayments are missed, the goods may be repossessed; alternatively, interest makes the total cost higher than the cash price.

questions.prompt: Discuss the factors a household should weigh when choosing a method of payment for a major household purchase, and assess the advantages and disadvantages of using credit to buy it. Refer to the protection given by the Consumer Credit Act 1995.
questions.model: Factors: cost (fees and interest), security (risk of loss and a payment record), convenience, availability (whether the retailer accepts the method), control over spending, and the size of the purchase. Advantages of credit: immediate use of goods, spreading of costs, fixed repayments, interest-free period on a credit card if paid on time. Disadvantages: high interest if not cleared, overspending, too many agreements, repossession under hire purchase, and not owning hire-purchase goods until the final payment. Consumer Credit Act 1995 (as amended): credit agreements must be in writing and set out the cost and repayment terms; advertisements must show the APR, total cash price, cost of credit and instalment details, so buyers can compare offers.
